summary: A queue: the tape is a row of blocks of ones separated by 0 0 1 0 0; at each visit of the left end the first block is taken apart and paid out, every other block gains 6 ones, and new small blocks are made at the right end (69,068 checks, no exception), so blocks age through the queue like the words of a tag system.
title: What is known about 1RB1RA_1RC---_1RD0LD_1LE1RF_0RA1LD_0RC0LC
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB1RA_1RC---_1RD0LD_1LE1RF_0RA1LD_0RC0LC.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open. The tape is a first-in first-out queue of blocks of ones; the law by which blocks move through the queue is checked in simulation at every visit of the first 3·109 steps, and the sweep moves are proved in Lean (kernel). How the new blocks at the right end are formed from the removed one is not yet worked out.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (B1); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 4,947 cells have been visited and 4,149 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: Growth shape: sqrt/sqrt
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.394). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.377).

claims.title: Sweep moves
claims.text: L A>1^n R → L 1^n A> R (n steps) and the zigzag L 1 D>(11)^n R → L (10)^n 1 D> R (6n steps), for every n, L, R.

claims.title: The queue law
claims.text: From one visit of the left end to the next the first block disappears, the second becomes the first with 8 more ones and every later block gains 6 ones: 69,068 checks in the first 3·10<sup>9</sup> steps, no exception.

claims.title: Queue length
claims.text: 16 blocks at step 8·10<sup>6</sup>, 25 at 1.4·10<sup>8</sup>, 38 at 8·10<sup>8</sup>, 51 at 2.9·10<sup>9</sup>; the first block has about 6 ones per block in the queue (289 at 2.9·10<sup>9</sup>).

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known. The queue law is measured; the rule that turns the removed front block into new blocks at the back, which is what a proof (or a halt) would hinge on, is not known yet.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows yet. This machine's tape is a queue. Blocks of ones wait in line; at each visit of the left end the first one is taken apart, every other block grows by six, and new small blocks join at the back. It looks like a tag system, a kind of process that can be very hard to predict.

facts.text: Checks of the queue law, no exception.
No halt in the C simulator; 4,947 cells visited.
No halt, proved in Lean; the first 10,000 by the kernel alone.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.394). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.377).
After 109 steps the tape spans 4,947 cells (1,276 left of the start, 2,602 right), with a density of 1s of 0.839.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

sections.heading: A queue of blocks
html:
At each visit of the left end the tape reads

1^n1 00100 1^n2 00100 … 00100 1^nk · tail

with the block sizes roughly decreasing from left to right, e.g. at step 2,999,129,327: 297 303 287 275 281 259 … 15 13 13 3 and a tail 1^3 (001)^4 1^8 (001)^4 1^5 (00111)^4 where new blocks are being built.

blockat the next visit
n1gone (taken apart)
n2first block, n2 + 8
ni, i ≥ 3ni + 6, one place forward
tailzero, one or two new small blocks

So every block keeps its place in line and grows by 6 per visit until it reaches the front: a block made with a few ones leaves the queue with about 6 × (queue length) ones. The ones of the removed block pay for the growth of all the others, and the leftover goes into the new blocks at the back; the tape grows by about one cell per visit, and the queue slowly gets longer (16 blocks at 8·106 steps, 51 at 2.9·109).

Patterns like 43 43 43 or 37 37 37 travel through the queue unchanged, since all blocks grow alike: the queue remembers what was appended, as in a tag system. Whether the machine halts depends on what the back of the queue is fed, which is decided by the size of the block taken apart at the front. The only halting transition is B on a 1, and B is entered only from A on a 0.
